A place I like to point to as a space habitat analog is the curiously named [Grin Grin Park] in Fukuoka Japan. The wintergarden dome complex of the park is an elaborate organic structure made by a very simple technique once used by German military engineers in WWII to construct vast earth-covered bomb-resistant aircraft hangars. Known as 'mound forming', its done by piling up mounds of gravel and sculpting them to a desired shape (within the limits of their material [angle of repose[(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle_of_repose)), arranging rebar on the surface of the mound, and then covering it in concrete. Once the concrete is cured, an earth berm is piled up for further protection and the interior of the now hardened shell is dug-out, the gravel re-used to make more structures. I've long speculated that similar techniques would be used in the construction of habitat on the Moon and Mars as this easily accommodates telerobotic construction and would allow built-up structures to merge seamlessly with excavated structures using the same general shapes and the same approaches to interior retrofit.

Having considered such structures for a long time, the Foster + Partners concept seems to me a little over-elaborate, undersized, and hampered by an essential irreparability. While there's nothing particularly wrong with the proposed fabrication method, the use of the pressure shell as a form and the merging of structures with the shell means that they are all made integral, yet the alloy and fabric materials have completely different duty-life from the built-up shell. So if and when they fail, the whole habitat is done. You can't remove and replace those elements and can only repair them with crude patches. What would be more practical is an approach similar to that once used by the US Amundson Base in Antarctica where a large area geodesic dome was used to enclose and shelter a changeable complex within it. (the dome was eventually removed when snow and ice built-up so much over many years it started to make the complex inaccessible) It's also quite possible to make these built-up structures pressurizable whole by coating their interiors with a thick inner shell of ceramic or epoxy compounds that would have duty life comparable to the outer shell. This would also allow the installation of arrays or grids of screw-in sockets that would allow for the freely-changeable retrofit attachment of mezzanines, wall covering panels, infrastructure hardware, and lighting.

Another sticking point with the Foster design is the skylights, which make little sense given the technology currently available. They are just big failure points and radiation leaks. Today we have at hand fiber optic heliostat systems far less expensive to make than such elaborate windowed cupolas. These devices can be setup anywhere on or around a habitat, tuned for optimal illumination, easily repaired, replaced, and reconfigured. They pipe natural sunlight into a structure by flexible cable to freely positioned emitters much like electric fixtures but without any electrical elements. Emitters can be fashioned in an endless variety of forms and could be used to illuminate the whole upper dome area as a 'synthetic sky' as well as serve as more conventional illumination, right down to linear grow lights for farming or even desk lamps, being switchable just like electric lights. Solid state, waterproof, and free of any bulbs to replace, they can be formed-in-place in walls, steps, walkways or placed in water. They could even be used as outdoor lighting around the habitat, being indifferent to the vacuum and extreme thermal conditions. They can also integrate with centralized electric light pumps for artificial lighting where needed (which saves power and greatly increases safety by eliminating electrical wiring) though the likely locations may need little supplemental lighting. These devices can also integrate in-line band-pass filters to reduce IR and UV radiation and direct it to high efficiency photovoltaic concentrators for electric power.

There seem to be a lot of obvious ways to simplify and improve on this moon base approach with stuff that's right at-hand.
